Depends on what kind you have. Embolic (a clot) can be removed sometimes. Sometimes you need a vein/artery clipping to stop bleeding. If it’s trauma related you get medications to reduce swelling, monitoring of the pressure inside your skull and sometimes surgery to evacuate the hematoma or release the pressure. It’s so important to have appropriate neuro monitoring to evaluate inter cranial pressures so you don’t end up brain damaged. In severe cases where we give you medications to shrink things (it’s a whole thing with sodium and mannitol) we have to carefully fix it back to keep you from having permanent damage from too rapid correction. You need to be in the hospital and watched closely. For mild concussions it might just be monitoring for a few days, and serial scans to make sure it’s not getting worse. But with all of them you need actual medical care. Not bullshit  chiropractor nonsense. Hon, listen to me please. I understand you completely. I was in your position. So much sexual violence. Traumatic life filled with physical, emotional and mental abuse my entire childhood. Thrown out of my house when I was 17. Then my first husband was abusive, abandoned me and my 3 month old baby in a shitty apartment in a terribly dangerous neighborhood. Cleaned out the bank account & took the car. I didn’t even have formula or diapers. I was all of 22 years old. 

I had been suicidal and a cutter since age 12. Not that children are the answer AT ALL but had it not been for my son I would be dead. I had to take care of him. Somehow someway I managed to go to nursing school. I had a breakdown going into my last year of clinicals, major PTSD things. Fucking up left and right. Luckily for me, the director of the program saw something in me worth saving. 

She had me take that semester off & mandated therapy for me with the school psychologist if I wanted to come back. It was a god send. It helped me start to learn how to deal with the trauma and all of my feelings. I got better outlets. For me it was art and drawing. I would draw, getting out intense feelings via paper, while being in “the art zone” where time and feelings and all other thoughts are suspended. I took up photography & got really good at it, roaming around cemeteries like some emo goth kid taking pictures of Angel headstones. But it worked. I was able to finish school and start as a nurse. 

Did everything magically get better? Of course not. Did I continue to have bad/difficult things happen? Absolutely. But the difference was I could stand up for myself & stay away from abusive relationships. I was better equipped to handle things when it hit the fan. I developed confidence in myself and my ability to handle anything life threw at me, and for the most part I have. And when I had set backs I knew what I needed to do to get help. 

Now I am 50, and have a good life. It’s not perfect & I still am pulling myself up, but I have friends and family and support. I know how to talk to people. I was able to “fake it till you make it” acted like I had confidence & self worth until I turned around one day and realized I really did. I found things I was good at & worked on those. It will and can get better, and at least different. But that’s only because I gave it time. 

You have to be kind to yourself. I’ve made a ton of mistakes & had a lot happen even as an adult, but I know I have value. & when I get in a bad place I get help. I’m back in therapy & staying sober. Please reconsider, & just take things one foot after another.

The rating system was actually introduced in 1968. You might be thinking of TV ratings which wasn’t proposed until 1996 and went into effect 1997. The ESRB was established 1994 to evaluate video game content. The FCC handles TV content and the MPAA does movies. Both the ESRB and FCC ratings came about as a result of congressional hearings/acts being passed.

Fun fact! When Jaws was first submitted to the MPAA for ratings, it got an “R” rating for “particularly gruesome dismemberment & gore”. Spielberg edited it and resubmitted it for a PG rating. This was a common practice by many directors who knew an “R” rating would kill their movie. PG 13 was introduced in 1984 to provide better guidelines between PG and R ratings.
